complexity_reason: Seven straightforward DATA steps reading CSV files with explicit LENGTH/INFORMAT declarations plus one PROC SQL sanity check. No macros defined or called, no includes, no joins, loops, arrays or dynamic table names; the only parameter is a single %LET controlling a column length. Short (66 lines) and has no upstream program dependencies.
business_description: This is the entry point of the analytics chain: it brings the bank's source extracts into the analysis environment. It loads customer master data, loans, loan repayments and card transactions, together with three control tables (client segments, reporting periods and macro parameters) that drive later processing. Each field is given a deliberate type and size and dates are read in a standard format, so that downstream lending, payments and risk reporting all start from consistent, well-typed data. A built-in check reports the longest customer name and the count of missing income values, highlighting the risk that a too-short name field would silently truncate customer names and corrupt reporting.
technical_description: Assigns STG and CTRL libraries, then uses seven DATA steps with FILENAME/INFILE (DSD, FIRSTOBS=2, TRUNCOVER) to read seven UTF-8 CSV files from &root/raw. Each step declares explicit LENGTH statements and yymmdd10. informats/formats for date columns, avoiding PROC IMPORT type guessing. A macro variable &name_len parameterises the customer_name length. Outputs ctrl.client_segments, ctrl.reporting_periods, ctrl.macro_parameters, stg.customers, stg.loans, stg.loan_payments, stg.card_transactions. A final PROC SQL prints max name length and missing income count.

complexity_reason: Single DATA step, 12 lines, one input and one output table, no macros, joins, loops or procedures. The only subtlety is the SAS missing-value comparison rule that silently assigns customers with no recorded income to the LOW income band, which must be replicated explicitly on migration.
business_description: Produces a cleaned customer master list for downstream use. Customer names are stripped of stray spaces and province codes are standardised to upper case so that customers can be grouped and matched consistently. Each customer is then placed in an income band - LOW, MID or HIGH - based on annual income, giving the bank a simple segmentation for customer management and analysis. Customers with no income recorded are explicitly flagged, and under current SAS behaviour they are treated as the lowest band, which means roughly fifteen customers are reported as LOW rather than being handled as unknown. This banding rule must be preserved deliberately when the process is rebuilt on a new platform.
technical_description: Reads stg.customers in a single DATA step. Applies STRIP to customer_name, UPCASE to province, sets income_missing via MISSING(annual_income), and derives a 4-character income_band using cascading IF/ELSE thresholds at 20,000 and 80,000. Writes out.customers_clean (500 rows). Note: SAS treats missing numerics as less than any value, so null incomes fall into 'LOW'; this must be coded explicitly in Python/Spark.

complexity_reason: A single PROC SQL statement with two joins, 11 lines, no macros, no includes, no loops and no dynamic logic; only notable subtlety is that the inner join silently drops loans whose customer is missing (800 in, 799 out).
business_description: This step builds the enriched loan view the bank uses downstream: every loan record is matched to its cleaned customer record so that the customer name, province and income band travel with the loan, and is then matched to the client segment lookup to attach the segment name and risk band. The result gives lending and risk users a single loan-level table that already carries who the borrower is, where they are and which segment and risk grade they fall into. Note that loans belonging to a customer who is not present in the cleaned customer file are dropped silently, so the enriched output contains fewer loans than the source (799 of 800).
technical_description: Single PROC SQL step. Reads stg.loans, inner-joins out.customers_clean on customer_id (dropping unmatched loans), then left-joins ctrl.client_segments on segment_code. Selects all loan columns plus customer_name, province, income_band, segment_name and risk_band, and creates out.loan_enriched. No data steps, macros, group-by or aggregation; depends on two upstream programs supplying the cleaned customer and segment tables.

complexity_reason: Only 13 lines with one PROC FORMAT and one DATA step, no macros, includes, joins or loops; a single input and single output. The only subtlety is the OTHER bucket capturing missing income as UNKNOWN, which must be replicated exactly when rebuilt as conditional logic outside SAS.
business_description: This step assigns every customer an income band label used in risk segmentation. Customers earning under 20,000 are flagged LOW, those between 20,000 and 80,000 MID, and 80,000 or more HIGH; anyone whose income is missing or outside these ranges is marked UNKNOWN. The banded view supports downstream risk assessment, customer segmentation and reporting where an exact income figure is not needed. Note that customers with missing income are treated as UNKNOWN here, whereas the upstream cleaning program classifies the same customers as LOW, so the two labels can disagree and should be reconciled before business use.
technical_description: Reads out.customers_clean. PROC FORMAT defines the 'incband' value format with ranges low -< 20000 = LOW, 20000 -< 80000 = MID, 80000 - high = HIGH, other = UNKNOWN. A DATA step applies it via PUT(annual_income, incband.) into a new $7 character column income_band_fmt and writes out.customer_risk (approx. 500 rows). No joins, macros or aggregation.

complexity_reason: Short (27 LOC, 1 data step, 2 procs) with no macros or includes, but the logic is order-dependent: NODUPKEY dedup, BY-group FIRST./LAST. processing, RETAIN plus a sum statement for running totals, multiple output datasets from one data step, and a delinquency threshold sourced from a control table via SELECT INTO rather than hard-coded. These stateful, row-order-sensitive constructs need careful re-expression in a set-based target platform.
business_description: This program turns raw loan repayment records into a picture of how well each borrower is keeping up with their loan. It first reads the bank's agreed late-payment threshold (days past due) from the central settings table, so the rule can be changed without touching code. Payments are then de-duplicated and reviewed in date order for each loan, producing a monthly payment record that shows the amount paid to date, the worst level of arrears reached so far, and whether the payment was late under the threshold. It also produces a one-line status per loan with total amount paid and maximum days past due, supporting arrears monitoring, collections prioritisation and downstream credit risk reporting.
technical_description: Reads the DPD_THRESHOLD value from ctrl.macro_parameters via PROC SQL SELECT INTO a macro variable. PROC SORT with NODUPKEY de-duplicates stg.loan_payments by loan_id and payment_date. A single BY-group DATA step uses RETAIN, a sum statement and FIRST./LAST. to compute cumulative paid, maximum days past due, a delinquency flag against the threshold and a YYYYMM period_id, writing detail rows to out.delinquency and one summary row per loan to out.loan_status.

complexity_reason: Ten lines, two standard summary procedures (MEANS and FREQ), a single input table, no macros, joins, loops or data steps; only nuance is that negative refund and zero amounts must be retained in the totals and averages.
business_description: Produces a management view of card activity by merchant category. For each merchant category it reports how many card transactions occurred, the total amount spent and the average transaction size, giving the bank a picture of where customers spend and at what ticket size. It also produces a cross-tabulation of merchant category against the fraud indicator, with counts and percentages, showing where suspected fraudulent transactions concentrate. Refunds (negative amounts) and zero-value transactions are deliberately included, so totals and averages reflect net spending rather than gross purchases; any replacement process must treat them identically to keep the figures comparable.
technical_description: Reads stg.card_transactions. PROC MEANS with NWAY classifies by merchant_category and summarises amount into n_txn, total_amount and avg_amount, writing out.card_summary (drops _TYPE_/_FREQ_). PROC FREQ cross-tabulates merchant_category by fraud_flag and writes counts and percentages to out.fraud_freq. Libraries stg and out are assigned via the &root macro variable. No data steps, joins or macro logic.

complexity_reason: Only 13 lines defining two small, self-contained macros with one PROC MEANS and one DATA step; no inputs, outputs, loops, joins or macro calls. The only dependency is that other programs (07, 08) %include and invoke it.
business_description: This is a shared building-block file rather than a business process in its own right. It provides two reusable routines that other reporting and analysis programs rely on: one that produces standard summary figures (count, total and average of a measure by a chosen grouping, such as a product or segment), and one that marks records that exceed an agreed threshold with a 'high' indicator. Centralising these routines means summary and threshold rules are applied consistently across the bank's reporting, reduces duplicated code, and makes any change to the definitions take effect everywhere at once. It creates no data and has no direct business output unless called by another program.
technical_description: Macro library with no inputs or outputs of its own. Defines %summarize(ds, class, var, out) which runs PROC MEANS NWAY to output n, sum and mean per class level (dropping _TYPE_/_FREQ_), and %flag_high(ds, var, threshold, out) which uses a DATA step to add a 0/1 high_flag where var exceeds the threshold. Included and called by downstream programs 07 and 08.

complexity_reason: Only 10 lines and a single PROC SQL, but the real logic sits in two macros pulled in via %include of program 06, and the threshold is data-driven from ctrl.macro_parameters into a macro variable. A converter must follow the include, both macro definitions and the control table to reproduce results, which raises effort above Simple.
business_description: Produces a loan portfolio summary for management reporting: total outstanding principal grouped by customer segment, with each segment marked when its total exceeds the bank's 'large portfolio' threshold. The threshold (5,000,000) is not hard-coded but held in a central settings table, so business users can change the definition of a high-exposure segment without changing code. The output gives one row per segment, supporting concentration monitoring and portfolio oversight discussions.
technical_description: Assigns ctrl and out libraries, %includes the shared macro library (program 06). PROC SQL reads param_value for 'HIGH_PRINCIPAL' from ctrl.macro_parameters into macro variable &high_principal. %summarize aggregates principal by segment_name from out.loan_enriched into out.portfolio_by_segment; %flag_high then compares total against the threshold, writing flagged results to out.portfolio_report (one row per segment).

complexity_reason: Short code (28 LOC) but high structural complexity: three levels of nested macros, an %include of the shared macro library (program 06), a loop driven by a control table read via SQL INTO, and output table names built at run time (out.period_summary_&pid), so the number of outputs changes with the data rather than the code.
business_description: This program produces the monthly payment summary used for delinquency reporting. It reads the bank's reporting calendar and picks up only the months flagged as active (currently September to December 2025). For each of those months it isolates that month's payment records from the delinquency dataset and produces totals and averages of payment amounts split between on-time and late payments, stored in one summary table per month. Because the list of months comes from a control table rather than from the code, business users can add or retire a reporting period simply by changing the active flag, and the corresponding monthly summary is created automatically - useful for month-end reporting cycles and back-filling prior periods.
technical_description: Reads ctrl.reporting_periods with PROC SQL SELECT INTO to build a space-separated macro list of active period_ids. %period_driver loops over the list with %do/%scan and calls %run_period, which subsets out.delinquency by period_id into a work table and invokes %summarize (from the %included 06_macro_library) grouped by delinquent_flag on payment_amount. Writes one dynamically named table per period: out.period_summary_202509 through _202512. MPRINT logged via MFILE.

complexity_reason: Five lines of code with a single PROC REG call, no macros, includes, loops or joins, one input and one output table, and a single upstream dependency.
business_description: This program quantifies how a loan's monthly payment relates to its core contract terms. Using the enriched loan portfolio, it fits a straightforward statistical relationship between the monthly payment and the loan's principal amount, interest rate and term in months. The resulting coefficients tell the bank, on average, how much the monthly payment changes for each additional unit of principal, each extra point of interest rate, and each additional month of term, together with a measure of how closely the fitted relationship matches actual payments. These estimates can support payment validation, pricing sanity checks and simple what-if estimates of instalment amounts for lending analysis.
technical_description: Assigns the out library and runs a single PROC REG on out.loan_enriched, fitting an ordinary least squares model of monthly_payment on principal, interest_rate and term_months with an intercept. Output is suppressed (noprint); the OUTEST= option writes one row of parameter estimates (intercept, three coefficients) plus the root mean squared error to out.reg_est. No data steps, macros or joins are involved.

complexity_reason: Only 16 lines with two procedures and no macros, loops or joins, so the code itself is short. Complexity comes from PROC FORECAST's double exponential smoothing with explicit options (METHOD=EXPO, TREND=2, WEIGHT=0.2, NSTART=12, LEAD=12) and the OUTFULL/OUTEST outputs, which have no direct Python equivalent and must be re-implemented by hand; it also depends on one upstream staging table that knowingly contains a duplicate payment row.
business_description: Produces the bank's monthly repayment picture: total loan payments received in each calendar month over a four-year window, then projects the next twelve months of expected repayments using an exponential smoothing model with a trend. This supports cash-flow planning, liquidity and funding forecasts, and gives collections and finance teams a view of whether repayment inflows are rising or falling. Because it reads the staging payments table as received, a known duplicate payment inflates one month slightly, so the reported actuals match the source system exactly rather than a cleaned version.
technical_description: Reads stg.loan_payments; PROC SQL buckets payment_date to month start via INTNX and sums payment_amount grouped and ordered by month, creating out.monthly_repay (48 rows). PROC FORECAST then applies METHOD=EXPO TREND=2 WEIGHT=0.2 NSTART=12 LEAD=12 on total_payment with ID month, writing out.fc (actuals, fitted and 12-month forecasts via OUTFULL) and out.fc_est (final internal parameter estimates).

complexity_reason: Only 22 lines with two PROC SQL steps, one parameter lookup into a macro variable, a single left join and a group-by aggregation; no macros, loops or data-driven logic. Mild complexity comes from depending on four upstream programs and five input tables, and from a correlated subquery filtering the forecast horizon.
business_description: Produces the one-page executive summary the bank uses to review its loan book. For each customer or product segment it reports how many loans exist, how many are delinquent (worst days-past-due above the late-payment threshold held in the central settings table rather than hard-coded), and the total principal outstanding. Alongside this it publishes the forward-looking repayment forecast, keeping only the months beyond the last month of actual repayment history so management sees genuinely future expected payments. Because it consolidates enriched loan data, delinquency status and the forecast, it is the final reporting layer; any error in the upstream loan, status or forecast processes surfaces in these figures.
technical_description: PROC SQL reads DPD_THRESHOLD from ctrl.macro_parameters into a macro variable. A second PROC SQL left joins out.loan_enriched to out.loan_status on loan_id and aggregates by segment_name (distinct loan count, count of loans exceeding the threshold, sum of principal) into out.exec_report. A further query selects FORECAST rows from out.fc with month greater than the maximum month in out.monthly_repay, writing out.exec_forecast.
